title: Reproductive Scouting and Unexpected Sex Expression

content.overview: Sex expression should be monitored as reproductive morphology across plant identity, position and time. Genetic sex-related information and observed flower expression are related but not interchangeable, and environmental/developmental context can influence expression.

vocabulary.definition: Flower bearing male reproductive structures that produce pollen.
Flower bearing female reproductive structures including stigmas and ovary.
Observed reproductive phenotype, which may reflect genetic, developmental and environmental influences.

sections.title: Scout structures, not labels
sections.body: Inspect nodes and developing inflorescences for reproductive morphology and record the plant ID/location rather than assuming a seed/clone label guarantees expression.

sections.title: Expression can be biologically plastic
sections.body: Modern cannabis sex-biology reviews describe genetic determination alongside hormonal and environmental influences on observed sex expression.

sections.title: Unexpected pollen structures change crop risk
sections.body: If pollen-producing structures appear in a seedless-flower crop, isolate/assess the affected scope promptly and preserve records for genetic/environmental investigation.

workedExamples: One unexpected staminate structure on a plant is a recorded reproductive event, not proof that every sibling will express identically.
A recurring expression pattern linked to one genotype across runs warrants breeding/source review as well as environmental review.
commonMistakes: Assuming feminized seed labels eliminate all scouting need.
Removing a suspect plant without recording identity/location.
Treating one environmental event as proven cause without replication.
content.practicalApplication: Add reproductive morphology to flowering scouting: plant ID, node/flower position, date, structure observed, photographs and action taken.
content.summary: Reproductive scouting protects crop goals and creates the evidence needed to distinguish genetic, developmental and environmental patterns.
